---
title: "One day – the cohabitation case"
subtitle: "Four parts of ninety minutes, with a facilitator"
---
The [case study](../../cases/cohabitation/index.qmd), which presents the original study, SCORE and the Multi100 project, the five reanalyses and the replications on which the day is built, is the place to start; its first three sections are the reading for before the day.

This is the one-day course on the cohabitation case. It brings the three strands of the course together, the computational tools, the statistics and the practices of open research, on a study in demography that compared the first cohabitations of American women begun in the early 1990s with those begun in the late 2000s, from two waves of the National Survey of Family Growth, and found that the couples of the later cohort married less often. Across the day you work as analyst no. 6 on a claim of the original authors (OAs) that five analysts reanalysed for Multi100. You reproduce the value that Multi100 recorded for one of them, find out what that value rests on, refit the published coefficient from the survey itself, write the estimand statement behind the claim, finish a causal graph that asks what it means that every woman in the data cohabited, work through a menu of defensible analyses, and then declare one of them in a shortened preregistration template before you run it. What you leave with is a report of your own, two marks on the class chart, one explored and one declared, and the place of your result among the 144 specifications on the curve of the claim.

The day runs as four parts of ninety minutes, with breaks of thirty, sixty and thirty minutes between them. Several of its steps are things that the class does together, such as everyone typing the $\chi^2$ statistic they have just reproduced and holding it back until the facilitator says go, so the day needs a facilitator. Some stretches of the slides are optional, a short tour of the toolchain and of R in the morning and a closer look at person-period data and discrete-time models in the afternoon, and the facilitator switches them on or off to suit the class.

| | What happens | Length |
|---|---|---|
| [Before the day](before.qmd) | Install R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), download the workspace, read the first three sections of the case study. | 1 to 2 hours, once |
| [Part 1 – Credibility and tools](part-1.qmd) | What a claim is for, why the field talks of a crisis, the evidence on reproduction, robustness and replication, and the toolchain; then you get running. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 2 – The claim, its estimand and its causal graph](part-2.qmd) | The paper and the five analysts, estimands and the causal-graph crash course; you write the estimand statement and finish the graph, which asks what keeping only women who cohabited does to a comparison of two periods. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration](part-3.qmd) | You reproduce the recorded result from the file of the analysts, find out why it points the wrong way, refit the published coefficient, then work the specification menu and put an exploratory mark on the class chart. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 4 – Multiverse, replication and preregistration](part-4.qmd) | The class reads its chart against the curve of 144, meets the two replications of the paper, which tested two different coefficients, and each participant declares one analysis, runs it and reports it. | 90 minutes |
| [After the day](after.qmd) | Where to go next in the companion curriculum. | as you like |
